questions.prompt: An anonymous visitor logs in using a session ID chosen before authentication. What most directly prevents session fixation?

choices.text: Keep the pre-login identifier because HTTPS prevents session fixation.
Issue a new session ID after authentication.
Retain the ID and change only its cookie expiration.
Encode the existing ID with Base64 before reuse.

questions.explanation: Renewing the identifier breaks an attacker-fixed session. Expiration, encoding and UI changes do not replace the attacker-known identifier.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Session identifiers require unpredictable randomness and renewal after authentication or privilege changes.

questions.prompt: A script cannot read an HttpOnly session cookie. Which risk can still remain?

choices.text: The script can issue requests with the attached cookie.
HttpOnly forces every request onto unencrypted HTTP.
HttpOnly stops the browser attaching the cookie at all.
HttpOnly removes the need to check resource permissions on the server.

questions.explanation: HttpOnly limits direct cookie access. It does not stop malicious scripts from making authenticated requests or replace TLS and authorization.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Secure restricts cookie transmission to HTTPS and HttpOnly blocks direct script reads without preventing authenticated requests.

questions.prompt: A logout endpoint deletes the browser cookie but leaves its session active on the server. What is missing?

choices.text: Increase cookie lifetime to make deletion more reliable.
Rename the session cookie without changing server state.
Keep the server session until the next successful login.
Invalidate the server-side session as well.

questions.explanation: A copied credential can remain usable if server state is not invalidated. Cookie deletion alone, renaming and delayed invalidation do not end that session.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Session idle and absolute timeouts and logout must be enforced by server-side invalidation.

questions.prompt: An API decodes a JWT payload and trusts its role without verifying the signature. What is the main flaw?

choices.text: A readable token cannot contain an expiration claim.
HTTPS makes every received token trustworthy by default.
Decoding does not establish token integrity.
Base64 decoding automatically checks the trusted issuer.

questions.explanation: A decoded payload is untrusted until integrity and intended-use checks succeed. Base64 and TLS do not replace token verification.

sources.title: REST Security Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: REST APIs verify JWT integrity and expected issuer, audience, expiration and not-before claims; a token header must not choose the verification algorithm.

questions.prompt: A user becomes an administrator during an existing session. Which change follows OWASP session guidance?

choices.text: Encode the administrator role into the existing opaque identifier.
Renew the identifier when the privilege level changes.
Retain the identifier because the user was already logged in.
Change only the session cookie name while retaining its value.

questions.explanation: Privilege changes require session renewal. Existing authentication does not remove fixation risk, and renaming or embedding privileges is not renewal.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Session IDs are renewed after privilege changes to prevent fixation.

questions.prompt: A session cookie needs protection from both plaintext transport and direct script reads. Which setting fits?

choices.text: Set both Secure and HttpOnly.
Set HttpOnly and send the session over ordinary HTTP.
Set Secure and permit every script to read its value.
Set a longer Max-Age instead of either attribute.

questions.explanation: Secure and HttpOnly address separate exposure paths. A long lifetime is not a confidentiality control.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Secure protects transport; HttpOnly restricts direct script reads.

questions.prompt: Which session identifier practices reduce guessing and fixation? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Treat Base64 encoding as a source of cryptographic randomness.
Encode the user’s role into the session ID instead of storing trusted state server-side.
Generate session IDs with a cryptographically secure random generator.
Regenerate the session ID when authentication changes its privileges.
Use an increasing customer number as the complete session credential.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Encoding changes representation rather than entropy. B is incorrect: Session identifiers should be opaque and meaningless; trusted state belongs on the server. C is correct: Unpredictability protects against session guessing. D is correct: Renewal prevents reuse of a pre-authentication identifier. E is incorrect: Predictable identifiers are not suitable authentication secrets.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Session identifiers require unpredictable randomness and renewal after authentication or privilege changes.

questions.prompt: Which session-cookie attribute statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Narrow cookie Domain and Path settings can limit exposure.
Secure restricts transmission to encrypted HTTPS connections.
HttpOnly prevents direct cookie reads through page JavaScript.
HttpOnly prevents all actions performed by injected same-origin scripts.
TLS makes unpredictable session identifiers unnecessary.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Avoiding unnecessary scope reduces where cookies are sent. B is correct: Secure protects cookie transport. C is correct: It restricts script access to the cookie value. D is incorrect: Injected code can still send authenticated requests. E is incorrect: TLS protects transport rather than identifier guessing.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Secure restricts cookie transmission to HTTPS and HttpOnly blocks direct script reads without preventing authenticated requests.

questions.prompt: Which session expiry controls belong on the server? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Enforce an idle timeout independently of client-side scripts.
Enforce an absolute timeout even for continuously active sessions.
Use a browser countdown as the sole authority for session validity.
A browser-side timeout alone makes the session invalid on the server.
Treat closing one browser tab as proof that every session ended.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Client controls can be bypassed. B is correct: It bounds total session lifetime. C is incorrect: The client cannot enforce server authorization. D is incorrect: Client-side timers cannot enforce server session validity. E is incorrect: Browser behavior does not guarantee server-side invalidation.

sources.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Session idle and absolute timeouts and logout must be enforced by server-side invalidation.

questions.prompt: Which JWT validation checks are appropriate for an API? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Check expected issuer and audience before accepting claims.
Check expiration and not-before time constraints.
Accept the algorithm advertised by any token without a local policy.
Treat a successfully decoded payload as an authenticated identity.
Verify integrity using a configured trusted verification method.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Claims must be intended for the API and trust domain. B is correct: Time claims constrain token validity. C is incorrect: The verifier must choose allowed algorithms independently. D is incorrect: Decoding is not cryptographic verification. E is correct: Signature or MAC verification protects authenticity.

sources.title: REST Security Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: REST APIs verify JWT integrity and expected issuer, audience, expiration and not-before claims; a token header must not choose the verification algorithm.
